CHAPTER 1.4 · LEARNING AREA 1

CHAPTER 1.4 · LEARNING AREA 1 · NOVEMBER

Quadratic equations and extreme values

When does the ball land? What is the largest area a fence can enclose? Which price brings in the most money? Questions like these lead to quadratic equations and to the vertex of a parabola. You learn to solve quadratic equations graphically, with the CAS, with the quadratic formula and in your head with Vieta’s theorem, and you find maxima and minima without any higher mathematics.

16 LESSONS4 UNITS1 LABCAS
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • find zeros of quadratic functions graphically and with the CAS, and interpret them
  • solve quadratic equations with the quadratic formula and distinguish all cases with the discriminant
  • solve simple quadratic equations without aids and check them with Vieta’s theorem
  • solve optimisation problems via the vertex and check the result against the situation

What is the $x$-coordinate of the vertex of $y = (x - 4)^2 - 9$?

$S(4, -9)$

Which positive number solves $x^2 = 49$?

$x = 7$, the second solution is $-7$.

When is a product $a \cdot b$ equal to zero?

That is the zero product property.

Complete: $x^2 - 6x + \ldots = (x - 3)^2$

$3^2 = 9$

PARABOLASVertex and zeros
UNIT 1WITH CAS · 4 LESSONS

1Zeros graphically and with the CAS

The ball lands when $h(t) = 0$. From the graph you read off the zeros $t = -1$ and $t = 5$. Only $t = 5$ fits the situation: the ball lands after 5 seconds. The solution $-1$ belongs to the parabola, but not to the throw, which only begins at $t = 0$.

A zero of the function $f$ is a solution of the equation $f(x) = 0$. You can already see how many there are from the vertex form: if the vertex of a parabola opening upwards lies below the $x$-axis, it cuts the axis twice; if it lies on it, it touches it once; if it lies above it, not at all.

KEY POINT · ZEROS OF QUADRATIC FUNCTIONS

Zeros of $f$ $\Leftrightarrow$ solutions of the equation $f(x) = 0$ $\Leftrightarrow$ intersections of the graph with the $x$-axis.

$f(x) = a(x - d)^2 + e$ has two zeros if $a$ and $e$ have different signs, exactly one for $e = 0$ and none if $a$ and $e$ have the same sign.

From the vertex form: $(x - d)^2 = -\tfrac{e}{a}$, so $x = d \pm \sqrt{-\tfrac{e}{a}}$ if $-\tfrac{e}{a} \geq 0$.

Zeros read off a graph are approximations. The CAS (solve, zeros) calculates exactly.

In context: check every solution. Negative times, lengths or numbers of items often drop out.

Symmetry helps: the zeros lie symmetrically about the vertex. With $-1$ and $5$ the vertex is at $t = 2$.

INTERACTIVE · VERTICAL THROW

Calculated with $g = 9.81\,\tfrac{\text{m}}{\text{s}^2}$: $h(t) = h_0 + v_0\,t - \tfrac{g}{2}\,t^2$. The landing time is the positive zero.

EXAMPLE 1 · FROM THE VERTEX FORM

Find the zeros of $f(x) = (x - 3)^2 - 4$.

$(x - 3)^2 = 4 \Rightarrow x - 3 = \pm 2$.

$x_1 = 1$, $x_2 = 5$, symmetric about the vertex $S(3, -4)$.

EXAMPLE 2 · HOW MANY?

How many zeros do $g(x) = 2(x + 1)^2 + 3$ and $h(x) = -(x - 2)^2 + 9$ have?

$g$: opens upwards, vertex above the axis: none.

$h$: opens downwards, vertex above the axis: two, namely $2 \pm 3$, that is $-1$ and $5$.

EXERCISES

Find the zeros: a) $(x - 1)^2 - 9$   b) $(x + 2)^2$   c) $-(x - 4)^2 + 1$   d) $(x - 1)^2 + 2$

a) $-2$ and $4$   b) only $-2$   c) $3$ and $5$   d) none

State without calculating how many zeros the function has: a) $3(x - 5)^2 - 1$   b) $-0.5x^2 - 2$   c) $-(x + 7)^2 + 0.1$

a) two   b) none   c) two

CAS Find the zeros of $f(x) = 0.3x^2 - 1.2x - 2$ to two decimal places. Read them off the graph first and compare.

$x_1 \approx -1.27$, $x_2 \approx 5.27$ (exactly: $2 \pm \sqrt{\tfrac{32}{3}}$).

A stone is thrown horizontally from a height of 20 m. Its height is $h(t) = 20 - 5t^2$. When does it hit the ground? Why does only one solution make sense?

$5t^2 = 20 \Rightarrow t = \pm 2$. Only $t = 2$ s, because the throw begins at $t = 0$.

Give a quadratic function whose graph opens downwards and which has the zeros $-3$ and $1$. Where is its vertex?

For example $f(x) = -(x + 3)(x - 1) = -(x + 1)^2 + 4$, vertex $(-1, 4)$. Any negative multiple works too; the vertex is always at $x = -1$.

TEST YOURSELF!

What is the larger zero of $f(x) = (x - 3)^2 - 4$?

$3 + 2$

How many zeros does $f(x) = 2(x + 1)^2 + 3$ have?

$a > 0$ and $e > 0$

$h(t) = 20 - 5t^2$. When is $h = 0$?

$t = 2$ s

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Quadratic formula and case analysis

If you complete the square once in general, you get a formula for every equation $x^2 + px + q = 0$: $$\left(x + \tfrac{p}{2}\right)^2 = \left(\tfrac{p}{2}\right)^2 - q$$ On the right is the discriminant $D$. If it is positive, you may take the root and get two solutions. If it is zero, only one. If it is negative, none.

KEY POINT · QUADRATIC FORMULA AND DISCRIMINANT

The equation $x^2 + px + q = 0$ has the solutions $$x_{1,2} = -\frac{p}{2} \pm \sqrt{\left(\frac{p}{2}\right)^2 - q}$$

With $D = \left(\tfrac{p}{2}\right)^2 - q$: $D > 0$ two solutions, $D = 0$ exactly one solution $x = -\tfrac{p}{2}$, $D < 0$ no real solution.

For $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ first divide by $a$, or directly $x_{1,2} = \dfrac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$.

“a” or “exactly one”? In mathematics “the equation has a solution” means: at least one. If you mean that there is only one, you say “exactly one”.

Signs: in $x^2 - 2x - 8 = 0$, $p = -2$ and $q = -8$. So $-\tfrac{p}{2} = 1$ and $-q = +8$.

INTERACTIVE · A FAMILY OF PARABOLAS

Change the parameter $a$ and watch when two zeros become one and then none. The case analysis is shown below.

EXAMPLE 3 · WITH THE FORMULA

Solve $x^2 - 2x - 8 = 0$ and $3x^2 - 12x + 9 = 0$.

$x_{1,2} = 1 \pm \sqrt{1 + 8} = 1 \pm 3$: $x_1 = 4$, $x_2 = -2$.

Divide by 3: $x^2 - 4x + 3 = 0$, $x_{1,2} = 2 \pm \sqrt{4 - 3}$: $x_1 = 3$, $x_2 = 1$.

EXAMPLE 4 · COMPLETE CASE ANALYSIS

For which $c$ does $x^2 + 4x + c = 0$ have two solutions, exactly one or none?

$D = 4 - c$.

$c < 4$: two · $c = 4$: exactly one ($x = -2$) · $c > 4$: none

EXERCISES

Solve with the formula: a) $x^2 - 7x + 12 = 0$   b) $x^2 + 2x - 15 = 0$   c) $x^2 - 10x + 25 = 0$   d) $x^2 + x + 1 = 0$

a) $3$ and $4$   b) $3$ and $-5$   c) exactly one: $5$   d) none ($D = \tfrac14 - 1 < 0$)

Solve: a) $2x^2 - 8x + 6 = 0$   b) $0.5x^2 + x - 4 = 0$   c) $-x^2 + 6x - 5 = 0$

a) $x^2 - 4x + 3 = 0$: $1$ and $3$   b) $x^2 + 2x - 8 = 0$: $2$ and $-4$   c) $x^2 - 6x + 5 = 0$: $1$ and $5$

For which $c$ does $x^2 - 6x + c = 0$ have a) exactly one solution, b) a solution, c) no solution?

“A solution” means: at least one.

$D = 9 - c$. a) $c = 9$   b) $c \leq 9$   c) $c > 9$

CAS A rectangle is 3 cm longer than it is wide and has an area of 40 cm². Set up an equation and solve it.

$x(x + 3) = 40 \Rightarrow x^2 + 3x - 40 = 0 \Rightarrow x = -1.5 \pm 6.5$. Only $x = 5$ makes sense: 5 cm by 8 cm.

For which $t$ does $x^2 + tx + 9 = 0$ have exactly one solution? Which is it in each case?

$\tfrac{t^2}{4} - 9 = 0 \Rightarrow t = \pm 6$. For $t = 6$, $x = -3$; for $t = -6$, $x = 3$.

TEST YOURSELF!

What is the larger solution of $x^2 - 2x - 8 = 0$?

$1 \pm 3$

For which $c$ does $x^2 + 4x + c = 0$ have exactly one solution?

$D = 4 - c = 0$

How many solutions does $x^2 - 3x + 2 = 0$ have?

$D = 2.25 - 2 > 0$: $1$ and $2$

UNIT 3WITHOUT AIDS · 4 LESSONS

3Solving in your head with Vieta’s theorem

Two numbers with sum 7 and product 12: $3$ and $4$. They solve $x^2 - 7x + 12 = 0$, because $(x - 3)(x - 4) = x^2 - 7x + 12$. So the sum and the product of the solutions are already in the equation. With product 12.25 there is only one number left, $3.5$, and with product 13 none at all.

Many equations are solved faster without the formula: if there is no $x$ without a square, you take the root. If the number without $x$ is missing, you factorise. And if the solutions are whole numbers, you find them in your head with Vieta.

KEY POINT · VIETA’S THEOREM AND SPECIAL CASES

If $x^2 + px + q = 0$ has the solutions $x_1$ and $x_2$, then $x_1 + x_2 = -p$ and $x_1 \cdot x_2 = q$, so $x^2 + px + q = (x - x_1)(x - x_2)$.

No constant term: $x^2 + px = 0 \Rightarrow x(x + p) = 0 \Rightarrow x = 0$ or $x = -p$ (zero product property).

No $x$-term: $x^2 = r \Rightarrow x = \pm\sqrt{r}$ for $r > 0$.

Vieta as a check: after every calculation check briefly: is the sum of the solutions $-p$ and the product $q$?

Do not divide by $x$: dividing turns $x^2 = 5x$ into $x = 5$, and the solution $x = 0$ is lost. Better: $x(x - 5) = 0$.

EXAMPLE 5 · IN YOUR HEAD

Solve $x^2 + x - 12 = 0$ with Vieta’s theorem.

Wanted: product $-12$, sum $-1$. One factor negative: $-4 \cdot 3 = -12$ and $-4 + 3 = -1$.

$x_1 = -4$, $x_2 = 3$

EXAMPLE 6 · BACKWARDS

Give a quadratic equation with the solutions $2$ and $-5$.

$-p = 2 + (-5) = -3$, so $p = 3$; $q = 2 \cdot (-5) = -10$.

$x^2 + 3x - 10 = 0$, equivalent to $(x - 2)(x + 5) = 0$.

EXERCISES

Solve without the formula: a) $x^2 - 16 = 0$   b) $2x^2 + 6x = 0$   c) $(x - 2)(x + 7) = 0$   d) $x^2 = 5x$

a) $\pm 4$   b) $2x(x + 3) = 0$: $0$ and $-3$   c) $2$ and $-7$   d) $x(x - 5) = 0$: $0$ and $5$

Solve in your head with Vieta: a) $x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0$   b) $x^2 + 6x + 8 = 0$   c) $x^2 - 2x - 15 = 0$   d) $x^2 + 4x - 21 = 0$

a) $2$, $3$   b) $-2$, $-4$   c) $5$, $-3$   d) $3$, $-7$

Give an equation $x^2 + px + q = 0$ with the solutions: a) $1$ and $6$   b) $-3$ and $-3$   c) $\tfrac12$ and $-2$

a) $x^2 - 7x + 6 = 0$   b) $x^2 + 6x + 9 = 0$   c) $x^2 + 1.5x - 1 = 0$

A rectangle has a perimeter of 34 cm and an area of 60 cm². How long are its sides? Solve without a calculator.

$a + b = 17$ and $a \cdot b = 60$: exactly Vieta’s conditions.

$a$ and $b$ solve $x^2 - 17x + 60 = 0$: $5 \cdot 12 = 60$ and $5 + 12 = 17$. 5 cm and 12 cm.

The equation $x^2 + px + 12 = 0$ has the solution $x_1 = 3$. Find the second solution and $p$ without using the quadratic formula.

$x_1 \cdot x_2 = 12 \Rightarrow x_2 = 4$, and $p = -(3 + 4) = -7$.

TEST YOURSELF!

What is the smaller solution of $x^2 + x - 12 = 0$?

$-4$ and $3$

$x^2 + px + q = 0$ has the solutions $2$ and $-5$. What is $q$?

$q = 2 \cdot (-5)$

$x^2 = 5x$ has the solutions $5$ and …?

$x(x - 5) = 0$

UNIT 44 LESSONS

4Optimisation problems

For the pen against the wall, let $x$ be the length of the two sides perpendicular to the wall. That leaves $40 - 2x$ metres of fencing for the third side. The area is $A(x) = x(40 - 2x) = -2x^2 + 40x = -2(x - 10)^2 + 200$. The vertex gives away the maximum: at $x = 10$ m the area is largest, at 200 m².

If the quantity that is to become as large or as small as possible depends quadratically on one variable, its largest or smallest value is at the vertex. You find it by completing the square or as the midpoint between the zeros.

KEY POINT · OPTIMISATION PROBLEMS
  1. Name the target quantity that is to be extreme, and make a sketch.
  2. Write down the constraint and use it to express the target quantity as a function of one variable.
  3. Give the sensible range of the variable.
  4. Find the vertex: for $a < 0$ it is the maximum, for $a > 0$ the minimum.
  5. Check the result against the situation and write a sentence as your answer.

Midpoint of the zeros: $A(x) = x(40 - 2x)$ is zero for $x = 0$ and $x = 20$. The vertex lies exactly in between, at $x = 10$.

Without derivatives: in Year 11 you learn a method for any function. For parabolas the vertex is enough.

INTERACTIVE · THE LARGEST AREA

Change $x$ and watch the picture and the graph. The grey point is the vertex of the parabola.

EXAMPLE 7 · LARGEST PRODUCT

Two numbers have the sum 20. When is their product largest?

$P(x) = x(20 - x) = -x^2 + 20x = -(x - 10)^2 + 100$.

Both numbers are 10, the product is 100.

EXAMPLE 8 · THE BEST PRICE

A cinema sells tickets at €8 to 300 visitors. Every reduction of €0.50 brings 30 more visitors. Which price brings in the most money?

After $x$ reductions: $E(x) = (8 - 0.5x)(300 + 30x) = -15x^2 + 90x + 2400 = -15(x - 3)^2 + 2535$.

Price €6.50, 390 visitors, takings €2535

EXERCISES

Which rectangle with a perimeter of 24 cm has the largest area?

$A(x) = x(12 - x) = -(x - 6)^2 + 36$: the square with side 6 cm, $A = 36$ cm².

A ball is thrown vertically upwards: $h(t) = 20t - 5t^2$. When is it highest, and how high is it then?

Zeros $0$ and $4$, vertex at $t = 2$: $h(2) = 20$ m.

A wire 60 cm long is bent into a rectangle. For which dimensions is the area largest? Explain why there is no sensible solution for the smallest area.

$A(x) = x(30 - x) = -(x - 15)^2 + 225$: a square 15 cm × 15 cm. The area becomes arbitrarily small when one side tends to 0; there is no smallest proper rectangle.

A bike hire shop rents out 60 bikes at €12 each per day. Every price increase of €1 loses 3 customers. Which price brings in the most money?

$E(x) = (12 + x)(60 - 3x) = -3x^2 + 24x + 720 = -3(x - 4)^2 + 768$: €16 per day, 48 bikes, €768.

A rectangle is placed in a right-angled triangle with legs of 6 cm and 8 cm, two sides on the legs and one corner on the hypotenuse. What is the largest the rectangle can be?

Put the legs on the axes. The hypotenuse is then the line $y = 6 - \tfrac34 x$.

$A(x) = x\left(6 - \tfrac34 x\right) = -\tfrac34(x - 4)^2 + 12$: rectangle 4 cm × 3 cm, $A = 12$ cm², exactly half the area of the triangle.

TEST YOURSELF!

What is the largest area $A(x) = x(40 - 2x)$?

$-2(x - 10)^2 + 200$

Two numbers have the sum 20. What is the largest their product can be?

$10 \cdot 10$

Which ticket price brings the cinema from example 8 the most money?

$8 - 3 \cdot 0.5 = 6.50$ €

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

Mixed practice without a calculator: a) $x^2 - 9x + 20 = 0$   b) $4x^2 - 25 = 0$   c) $x^2 + 8x + 16 = 0$   d) $3x^2 - 12x = 0$

a) $4$, $5$   b) $\pm\tfrac52$   c) $-4$   d) $0$, $4$

Connecting with chapter 1.1: solve the equation with a root $\sqrt{x + 6} = x$ and check.

Squaring: $x^2 - x - 6 = 0$, so $x = 3$ or $x = -2$. Check: $\sqrt{9} = 3$ ✓, $\sqrt{4} = 2 \neq -2$. $L = \{3\}$

Calculate the points of intersection of the parabola $y = x^2 - 2x - 3$ with the line $y = x + 1$.

$x^2 - 3x - 4 = 0 \Rightarrow x = 4$ or $x = -1$: $S_1(4, 5)$, $S_2(-1, 0)$.

A rectangle is to be inscribed in a circle with radius 5 cm. Show that for its area $A^2 = x^2(100 - x^2)$ if $x$ is one side. For which $x$ is $A^2$, and hence $A$, largest?

The diagonal is the diameter. Substitute $u = x^2$: $A^2 = u(100 - u)$ is a parabola in $u$.

The other side is $\sqrt{100 - x^2}$ (Pythagoras, chapter 3.1). $u(100 - u) = -(u - 50)^2 + 2500$, maximum at $u = 50$: $x = \sqrt{50} \approx 7.07$ cm. The largest rectangle is a square with $A = 50$ cm².

EXCURSIONHISTORY

How al-Khwarizmi completed a square

Around 825 the scholar Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi wrote a textbook in Baghdad on calculating with equations. One word of its title, al-jabr, became our word algebra. His most famous example: “A square and ten of its roots make thirty-nine.” Today we write $x^2 + 10x = 39$.

Al-Khwarizmi solves it with a picture. He draws a square with side $x$ and places a rectangle $5 \times x$ against each of two sides, together the $10x$. The figure has the area 39. In the corner a square $5 \times 5$ is missing. If you add it, you get a large square with area $39 + 25 = 64$, so with side $8$. Hence $x + 5 = 8$ and $x = 3$. That is exactly completing the square, only drawn instead of calculated. He did not know negative solutions.

Source: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, al-Kitāb al-muḫtaṣar fī ḥisāb al-ǧabr wa-l-muqābala, Baghdad around 825. English edition: F. Rosen, The Algebra of Mohammed ben Musa, London 1831.

LOOKING BACKTHE ESSENTIALS AT A GLANCE

ZERO = SOLUTION

The zeros of $f$ are the solutions of $f(x) = 0$. Check them in context.

$(x - 3)^2 - 4 = 0$: $1$ and $5$

QUADRATIC FORMULA

$x_{1,2} = -\tfrac{p}{2} \pm \sqrt{\left(\tfrac{p}{2}\right)^2 - q}$

$x^2 - 2x - 8 = 0$: $1 \pm 3$

DISCRIMINANT

$D > 0$ two, $D = 0$ exactly one, $D < 0$ no solution.

$x^2 + 4x + c$: $D = 4 - c$

VIETA

$x_1 + x_2 = -p$, $x_1 \cdot x_2 = q$ · factorise, take roots

$x^2 + x - 12 = (x + 4)(x - 3)$

EXTREME VALUES

Set up the target function, find the vertex, check against the situation.

$x(40 - 2x)$: maximum $200$ at $x = 10$
